situation: The author wanted to enter a different field but lacked qualifying experience and faced a below-standard salary offer.
choice: They accepted the lower-paying job offer to gain experience in the new field.
outcome: They learned a lot, grew professionally, and three years later landed a position paying 40% more.
main_reason: The role was an opportunity to transition into a new field despite lacking prior experience.
advice: Focus on learning and building achievements for a few years, then negotiate more aggressively for your next position.
quote: Three years later (which were fantastic years: I have learned a lot, participated in a great projects and grew professionally really high) I've got a job that was about 40% more that what I had at the time (and put me a bit higher than standard for a more senior position that I had in my 1st company).
author: AlexanderM

situation: The author decided to leave their job at a small company and subsequently received an unexpected pay raise.
choice: The author accepted the raise and expressed appreciation, but still chose to leave for another career opportunity.
outcome: They left on good terms, maintaining positive relationships with both former employers without burning any bridges.
main_reason: The author's decision to leave was not financially motivated, so the raise did not alter their plans.
advice: Accept a raise with gratitude if offered, even when intending to leave, while remaining committed to the planned career move.
quote: How I handled it clearly didn't badly burn any bridges.
author: TOOGAM

situation: The author started in an entry-level call center job with limited experience.
choice: They repeatedly changed jobs, leveraged short-term roles, and started a business to advance their career.
outcome: They steadily increased their earning power over time, eventually landing a $100,000 position.
main_reason: They wanted to take advantage of the system and maximize their income by using every job as a stepping stone.
advice: Treat every job as a stepping stone, job hop early in your career, and rely on demonstrable skills rather than references.
quote: After just 4 months at the $95K job, I re-contacted the person whose job offer I turned down 3 times only to finally accept an offer with them for $100K.
author: Mister Mister

situation: Started freelancing from home after four years of office work and struggled to build a work pattern
choice: Went freelance, returned to a 9-to-5 after three months, then came back to freelancing years later
outcome: Built better habits and now has more than five years of remote work experience
main_reason: Freedom to set their own schedule and work remotely
advice: Build a routine, exercise, work from cafes or co-working spaces, and set deadlines
quote: I have 5+ years working remotely experience now. I would not change it.
author: christopherros

situation: Moved to a new country and entered the software industry as a consultant
choice: Broke in by charging about 80% of what big companies charged instead of working for much less
outcome: Four years later was one of the most expensive people in the country in their niche
main_reason: Lower overheads let them undercut big firms and still earn well
advice: Success needs many skills beyond technical ones, plus self-confidence; pricing at 50% of market looks desperate and most who try fail
quote: I broke into the industry in a new country at 80% of what big companies charged (I didn't have their overheads so it was a lot of money), about 4 years later I was one of the most expensive people in the country in my niche.
author: Kilisi

situation: Engineer who moved into web development, taking a big pay and benefits cut
choice: Made a complete career transition from engineering to web developer
outcome: Does not regret the change, though favorite coworkers and the mentor left and a new lead brought anxiety five months in
main_reason: Wanted the change and enjoyed learning and supportive coworkers
quote: Even though I took a massive pay and benefits cut from my previous engineering job, I don't regret making this change at all.
author: Rachel Marquez

situation: Had turned down one job offer and had several others pending, so leaving the company was likely
choice: Told their boss they were leaving
outcome: Boss was not surprised and the relationship stayed good two years later
main_reason: Better opportunities elsewhere
advice: Keep it positive and professional; good relationships with competent people open doors
quote: I told him, he wasn't surprised, and we still have a great relationship - 2 years later we still touch base and keep in contact and I count that as an overall career win.
author: bethlakshmi

situation: Outsourced developer on projects where teams cared more about getting work done cheaply than about code quality
choice: Rejected several job offers, including a promotion, and resigned once for that reason
outcome: Does not regret it; one resignation set off others and the company changed how it worked
main_reason: Team culture did not value quality work
advice: If the culture does not fit how you want to work, this is not the job for you
quote: I have personally rejected multiple project/job offers (even one promotion) precisely for this reason and looking back, I don't regret them.
author: Xeverous

situation: Had a new job offer and was asked by their employer to stay with a counteroffer
choice: Accepted the counteroffer instead of leaving
outcome: Stayed happy, was not pushed out or questioned about loyalty, left three years later, and the old employer became a client
main_reason: Happy with the job and the counteroffer
advice: Weigh the pros and cons of each path and pick the one that makes the most rational sense
quote: I once accepted a counteroffer, and I do not regret having done so.
author: Panda Pajama

situation: Faced a practice at work they considered unethical
choice: Stood up against it, then quit with no new job lined up when things became miserable
outcome: Years later a former colleague praised them for standing up for what is right, which made it worth it
main_reason: Standing up for ethics
advice: Doing the right thing can cost you, but it is worth taking the hit
quote: The whole nasty mess was worth it just for that moment.
author: B. Goddard

situation: Wanted a break from work before moving on
choice: Quit their job and took a four-month break while preparing for interviews
outcome: Interviewed at 18 companies, the gap was never a problem, and received offers
main_reason: Wanted time off and time to prepare for interviews
advice: A short gap in your CV is not an issue; tell the truth about wanting time off
quote: The break itself was great and preparing for interviews was also much easier this way, I could go on 2 interviews a day and prepare/practice a lot.
author: farkas

situation: Part-time worker at a village shop with a horrible boss who blamed others
choice: Quit on the spot with no notice
outcome: Later jobs never asked about it; no consequences
main_reason: Boss was unfair and constantly changed his mind
advice: Normally give notice and put the job on your CV, but with no contract a few days is enough
quote: I certainly don't regret quitting with no notice
author: David

situation: Intern doing real full-day work under a boss who taught them a lot, unhappy with the pay
choice: Rejected the pay rudely and made a hasty exit
outcome: Says it was a mistake with several downsides beyond the money
main_reason: Unhappy with the pay despite a great boss
advice: Try to solve the actual problem instead of taking an extreme step; companies invest in people and good relationships make things workable
quote: I made the mistake and it has several downsides
author: Abhirath Mahipal

situation: Moving far away and wanting to keep the job
choice: Asked the boss to let them work remotely instead of quitting
outcome: Signed a contract to finish the year and was still working for the company three years later, though sometimes with a pay cut
main_reason: Wanted to keep the job after moving
advice: Listen to your boss's concerns and be ready to negotiate salary, benefits and hours
quote: Three years later, I'm still working for them.
author: user8365

situation: Worked in corporate jobs and saw how incompetent some companies are
choice: Quit corporate work and returned to graduate school
outcome: Is amazed at the high level of competence in academia
main_reason: Frustration with competence in corporate work
advice: Some companies have competence and some do not; get experience anyway
quote: Years later, I have quit corporate work and returned to graduate school.
author: Astor Florida

situation: Five years into a career with several short stints after quitting two bad jobs and being caught in a bankruptcy and a layoff
choice: Quit their first two jobs after a little over a year each
outcome: Does not regret it because the places were bad, but now worries about a quitter mindset in the fifth job
main_reason: The workplaces were really bad for different reasons
quote: When I look back, I don't regret it at all, the places were really bad for different reasons.
author: user4408343

situation: Near burnout in a toxic workplace with constant finger-pointing and falling evaluations
choice: Quit and accepted the first new job offer
outcome: The new job is a perfect fit with a supportive team, though the salary is low
main_reason: Burnout from a toxic workplace
quote: So, the job is really a perfect fit for me.
author: dragonNoir

situation: PhD student who lacked soft skills like time management and resilience and struggled with slow progress
choice: Quit the PhD eight months after starting
outcome: Moved into teaching and now wants to transition to a technical field; stands by the decision but worries how to explain it
main_reason: Slow progress and struggling to manage themselves
quote: I know the reasons in my head for dropping out of the PhD are sound
author: user71909

situation: Left a job of almost 10 years for a higher-paid role right out of school, with 12 months to pass a certification exam offered only twice a year
choice: Took the new job, which they later left
outcome: Now has to explain a messy departure from a job they liked, and learned to get things in writing
main_reason: Attracted by a much higher salary
advice: Get everything in writing and do not jump into something just to leave or be tempted by a bigger salary
quote: I have learned so much throughout this process about getting things in writing and not jumping into something else just for the sake of leaving and not being tempted by larger salaries
author: valerie

situation: PhD student whose advisor could not secure meaningful funding
choice: Submitted the work as a Master's thesis and moved to another PhD program with a better stipend
outcome: Finished the PhD, got two postdocs, and is now a tenured full professor
main_reason: Funding problems
advice: Switching universities over funding is a cleaner reason than conflicts with advisors or labmates
quote: I had no problems gettting postdocs (2) and I'm now a tenured full professor.
author: Cheery

situation: Researcher who moved completely from one field to another
choice: Switched fields between their PhD and later work
outcome: Succeeded but it took a lot of work to make up for missing education in the new area
main_reason: Wanted to work in a different field
advice: Switching fields is rare; focus on technical skills, which mattered more than topic knowledge for postdoc applications
quote: while I don't regret switching, it was (and still is) a lot of work making up for essentially missing education in the area you work in.
author: LonLon

situation: Researcher in the last year of a PhD, unhappy with the place and with the scientific supervision
choice: Quit and changed after 4 years and 2 months, despite having five papers
outcome: Says they would stay and finish the PhD if they could go back
main_reason: Unhappy with the place and lack of proper supervision
advice: Finish the PhD in the current place, then look for other research opportunities
quote: if i have the opportunity to go back in time and make that decision again, I would stay and finish my PhD and then look for other research opportunities to satisfy myself.
author: Zalit Forn

situation: Wanted a doctorate but decided to work in industry first
choice: Worked first and applied for the doctorate much later
outcome: Applied again at 33 after 12 years, lost academic references, and thinks they are no longer an ideal candidate
main_reason: Working first has several advantages
advice: Working first can be a long shot with low payoff; internships may be a better route to industry experience
quote: Ultimately, life got complicated and busy, and it took me 12 years to apply for the doctorate I've long sought.
author: Iiridayn

situation: Graduated into a terrible academic job market while highly thought of by peers and faculty
choice: Changed fields from math to computer science and searched for jobs for several years
outcome: Forty years later their goals were largely met
main_reason: Terrible academic job market
advice: Deal with the emotional letdown, ignore age as a factor, and take heart that your advisor believes in you
quote: But, forty some years later, my goals were largely met.
author: Buffy

situation: One year into a PhD in Europe when their pregnant wife had a terrible car accident
choice: Left the PhD program and moved countries to restart
outcome: Finished the PhD in Australia with good standing and stayed on good terms with the old supervisor
main_reason: Needed to leave behind painful memories after the accident
quote: looking back, I couldn't be happier with my decision to leave.
author: Pioneer83

situation: Physics graduate weighing industry money against an academic path
choice: Finished the PhD, took time for a startup, and later worked in consulting alongside a modest academic career
outcome: Likes what they do, has a good family life, and is glad about the academic career they had
main_reason: Wanted to do well and like their work
quote: But my family is well, the kids are good, and I like what I'm doing - and I'm glad I had the modest academic career I did have.
author: ashin

situation: Grad student who found research stressful and lost their social and family life, with no workable dissertation topic after four years
choice: Quit the PhD after four years of coursework
outcome: Found a good job at a good company; nobody cared that they did not finish
main_reason: Research did not fit their personality and was grueling
advice: There is no shame in not finishing a PhD
quote: Almost 6 years later I am extremely happy with my decision though it was extremely scary at the time
author: Happy Ex PhD student

situation: Thrown off the most prestigious project at a top lab
choice: Spent three years at another institution abroad, then came back and finished the degree
outcome: Met their spouse abroad, completed the degree with a new supervisor, and the elite degree helped their career
main_reason: Lost their place on the project
advice: If you love research but dislike the atmosphere, transfer labs or institutions; if you dislike open-ended research, try business, law, medicine or consulting
quote: The elite degree has definitely helped my career.
author: Joanna Bryson

situation: First-year PhD student whose advisor was emotionally abusive and unethical
choice: Switched labs after the first year with the department chair's help
outcome: Moved to another lab while the old advisor later lost five students in two years
main_reason: Abusive advisor
advice: Leave quietly and frame it as a lack of research fit; play your hand shrewdly
quote: Honestly, I think the best thing to do is leave the lab and go somewhere else.
author: bfoste01

situation: Undergraduate who wanted a more competitive school and a different focus
choice: Transferred schools during undergrad
outcome: Got into the more competitive school but needed an extra year; was proud of being pushed harder, though opportunities were similar and starting over was lonely
main_reason: Wanted a more competitive school
advice: Stay where you are and find a mentor; a solid GPA and individual drive count for more than names
quote: When I finally graduated, I was proud that I was pushed harder and learned more, but found that many of the same opportunities existed despite having gone to a better university.
author: Twitch

situation: Worried a Master's degree in computer science might make them overqualified
choice: Completed an MSc in Computer Science
outcome: Switched jobs and was interviewed by four large companies specifically seeking Master's graduates; financially better off
main_reason: Better job prospects
advice: The rumor that a Master's makes you overqualified is wrong
quote: I received an MSc last year in Computer Science, and I no longer eat ramen unless I want to.
author: Compass

situation: First-year physics PhD student who lost their passion for academia
choice: Left the PhD, worked at a tech startup for about 1.5 years, then went into freelance analytics consulting
outcome: Enjoys the freedom of working from home and the work, though sometimes wonders what would have happened
main_reason: Lost passion for the academic world
quote: Though I do often wonder about what would have happened if I stayed, I don't regret it.
author: user7007

situation: PhD student who loved the people, the science and the teaching but realized they would leave academia
choice: Did the PhD anyway and later started their industry job
outcome: Started working later than peers, which has pros and cons, but has no regrets about the PhD years
main_reason: Enjoyed the PhD years
advice: Consider your joy so you can say years later that the choice was good for you
quote: I do not regret one minute spent on my PhD, even if it meant starting in the job later (which has both advantages and disadvantages).
author: WoJ

situation: Physics PhD student in the early 90s who wanted to push new computer methods into a slow-changing department
choice: Left academia for industry
outcome: Found they could do fantastic things in industry and earn about five times as much
main_reason: The academic system was hard to change and industry paid far more
advice: A good supervisor lets you drive and helps you navigate academic politics
quote: I left academia because the neo-medieval system was hard to change and I realized that I could do fantastic things in the industry as well (and be paid 5 times what I would be in academia).
author: WoJ

situation: Knew from the start of the PhD they would leave academia and was already working as a consultant
choice: Did the PhD without career pressure and then went into industry
outcome: Had a rewarding, relaxed PhD with good research and lasting friendships
main_reason: Industry paid far better and academic hierarchy was unappealing
advice: Not depending on academia for a career lets you enjoy research and teaching
quote: I would not change a bit if I was to do it again.
author: WoJ

situation: Physicist who was not a top scientist but loved technology and teaching, with severe doubts about leaving
choice: Left academia for IT in industry about 20 years ago
outcome: Now works in a highly innovative industry with better pay, no grant hunting, and better work-life balance
main_reason: Better money, no funding stress and less medieval culture
advice: Consider teaching at a university as a side activity
quote: I moved forward, though, and I am now part of a highly innovative industry and do not regret it.
author: WoJ

situation: Enjoyed the PhD but knew it could not last forever
choice: Moved from the PhD into industry
outcome: Has a permanent contract, no funding worries, more responsibility, and never wanted to go back
main_reason: Wanted stability and a new challenge
advice: Go to industry and find out there are cool jobs there too
quote: Now I don't have to think about funding, I have a permanent contract, still doing cool stuff (but completely different), I took over a lot more responsibility, and never wanted to go back.
author: usr1234567

situation: Worked in software industry after a master's and then wanted to return to study
choice: Went back to do a PhD after working in industry
outcome: Industry experience helped in applied projects and in hiring for senior posts; later started their own company
main_reason: Wanted to combine real-world experience with research
advice: Industry experience gives an entrepreneurial attitude; the only downside is being one of the oldest PhD students
quote: I did exactly that and I think that was a great thing.
author: walkmanyi

situation: Started an industry-funded PhD that never felt like their own project, with a bad supervisor
choice: Quit the PhD
outcome: It came at a huge cost, but years later they returned to do their own project in a different field and it was the best decision they made
main_reason: The project was not theirs and the supervisor was bad
advice: Weigh it on balance; you can also switch projects or take leave
quote: So I bailed and never looked back.
author: Collega

situation: PhD student who went through a roughly two-year crisis
choice: Pushed through, finished the PhD, and left academia for industry
outcome: Happy in an industry job with faster feedback and more teamwork
main_reason: Industry offers more collaboration and planned progress than academia
advice: Most PhD students have a crisis; working through it can be worth it
quote: I don't regret to have invested the two difficult years.
author: usr1234567

situation: Biochemistry graduate who spent five years on a PhD
choice: Completed the PhD
outcome: Says it was not worth it and that most people with a PhD regret doing it
main_reason: Wanted the PhD as a credential
advice: Do not do a PhD unless you need it for a job; you can quit anytime and in STEM leave with a master's
quote: After getting a PhD after five years in Biochemistry, I can say don't do a PhD.
author: hack 91372

situation: PhD student who enjoyed the people, the parties and some research
choice: Did the PhD even though it was not very useful for industry
outcome: Remembers it as some of the best years of their life and met their wife there
main_reason: Enjoyed the community and student life
advice: Seize the day and stop worrying about insignificant things
quote: Some of the best years of my life.
author: WoJ

situation: Software engineer in a first full-time job who also wanted a master's degree
choice: Did a thesis-based MSc in Software Engineering while working full time
outcome: Was mentally drained every day and could have finished the thesis a year faster without the job
main_reason: Wanted a master's without leaving work
advice: Avoid doing a thesis master's while working full time if you can; it takes lots of self-motivation
quote: I did this with a thesis-based MSc in Software Engineering. It was a terrible idea.
author: Catsunami

situation: Started a PhD planning to go into industry where a PhD would be needed, but it was not going well or enjoyable
choice: Stuck with it for more than three years, then quit and changed career direction
outcome: Has worked for 35 years and the PhD never mattered to their career
main_reason: The PhD was not enjoyable and did not suit their career
advice: Research what career you want and whether a PhD helps; do not stay when you know it is not working
quote: Do I regret giving up? Very very rarely. Do I regret having started it? Rarely.
author: houninym

situation: PhD student isolated in a different research center with two supervisors who paid more attention to other students
choice: Stayed three years hoping they would stop messing them around
outcome: Suffered stress and sorrow from wasted work and little guidance, and regrets staying
main_reason: Hoped the supervisors would change
advice: Quit as early as you can and start a PhD elsewhere where people appreciate you
quote: what I regret the most is to stay hoping they will stop messing me around.
author: Juan Luis Gómez González

situation: Engineering graduate who did not go straight on to a PhD
choice: Never got a PhD
outcome: At 68 regrets it and says the best time to do a PhD is right after the bachelor's
main_reason: Few people who plan to work first actually return for a PhD
advice: If you are thinking about a PhD, the best time is probably immediately after your bachelor's degree
quote: I never got a PhD and I regret it.
author: Nicole Hamilton

situation: History PhD student who felt they were wasting their life while friends built careers
choice: Left the PhD rather than spend 3-4 more years of nearly unpaid labor
outcome: Three years later is a junior software engineer in a rewarding, well-paid job
main_reason: Low pay and poor odds of a professorship
advice: Learn to code; it is a highly employable skill, even among scientists
quote: Three years later, I am now a junior software engineer. My job is challenging, rewarding, and a source of pride.
author: Umbrella_Programmer

situation: Got a US PhD in 2009 right after the financial crash and had to leave the academic track and the country for personal reasons
choice: Moved out of academia and built a freelancing career
outcome: By 2018 was freelancing, travelling the world and earning good money, using skills from the PhD
main_reason: Forced by personal circumstances and a tough job market
advice: Do not despair; work hard at another opportunity because careers often pick you
quote: Now let's roll forward to 2018. I am in a lovely profession, freelancing, travelling the world and making good money for myself.
author: curious_cat

situation: PhD student in algebra who found the work hard on their mental health
choice: Left academia for a software developer job after finishing the PhD
outcome: Works on applied AI for agriculture and still plans to become a professor someday
main_reason: Theoretical research was taxing and they wanted more applied work
quote: I found a job where I can use my skills to really help people/the climate/...
author: Dirk

situation: Student with a poor PhD supervisor who did not leave the lab early
choice: Stayed with the supervisor instead of switching labs
outcome: Is burning out and was forced to quit the PhD
main_reason: Trusted the supervisor's prestige and citations
advice: Ask current students and alumni before joining, trust your gut, and switch labs if you see red flags
quote: regret not doing that right decision since earlier time
author: user39171

situation: Software developer who disliked always solving other people's problems
choice: Left industry to return for a neuroscience PhD
outcome: Works on questions that interest them but still wonders about the road not taken
main_reason: Wanted to work on their own questions
advice: Talk to your advisor about second thoughts; consider working a few more years first
quote: I don't know that I regret it, but I do often wonder what my life would have been like if I stayed in industry.
author: jerlich

situation: Wanted to stay near their girlfriend, keep their sport, and avoid military service, with funding and an interesting project available
choice: Entered a PhD program instead of looking for a job
outcome: The PhD led to a postdoc and a 27-year industry career; married their girlfriend and raised four children
main_reason: Stay with partner and team, funding, and an interesting project
quote: The PhD was fun, led to a postdoc, then to a role in industry.
author: Floris

situation: Wanted a PhD while holding a full-time job and a part-time job
choice: Did the PhD part-time around 44 hours of work a week
outcome: Very hard work but rewarding, with low stress and useful transferable skills
main_reason: Loved the subject
advice: Set weekly goals, tell your employer and advisor, take time off, and keep sleep and social time
quote: I can say, looking back, it is very hard work, but can be very rewarding.
author: user70612

situation: Part-time master's student working full time whose wife was put on bed rest during a pregnancy
choice: Withdrew from classes to focus on family and finished the master's nine years later
outcome: Graduated after being laid off and finding no hiring, and does not regret putting family first
main_reason: Needed to care for their wife and children
advice: The PhD will not always be there; education moves down the priority list as responsibilities grow
quote: I absolutely don't regret taking the time to focus on my family.
author: DLS3141

situation: Student in a prestigious program earning $80/hour on contract work who felt the degree was just a piece of paper
choice: Dropped out to work and plan a business
outcome: Six years later is applying to grad school again because most jobs are dull and prospects are limited without a degree
main_reason: Felt the degree was pointless and wanted to work and start a business
advice: Finish what you started; without the degree most opportunities beyond grunt work are closed
quote: But here I am, 6 years later, applying for grad school to give it another go.
author: CaptainCodeman

situation: Programmer who started working during college and got good jobs early
choice: Skipped finishing the master's to work
outcome: Has a few years' more experience than classmates who finished, though some peers got great internships at big companies
main_reason: Early job offers and experience
advice: Ask whether the PhD is needed for the job you want, whether money will be an issue, and how likely you are to resume later
quote: I also have a few years of experience ahead of my former colleagues that didn't do what I did and finished their studies, but I don't regret my decision.
author: Vlad Preda

situation: Master's graduate in Sweden who did not get PhD positions when they first applied
choice: Took a break, moved to Germany, and worked in industry software design for 10 months before starting a PhD
outcome: Industry and open source experience helped them win the PhD position; they graduated and are now writing their own grant
main_reason: Did not get a PhD position the first time
advice: A break with relevant industry experience can strengthen a PhD application, especially in Europe
quote: For me, this all worked out well.
author: Mikael Vejdemo-Johansson

situation: Master's student who started the PhD on the Monday after the last exam on Thursday, in a new country with a breakup
choice: Started the PhD straight away without a break
outcome: Became ill right away and had a stressful start
main_reason: Wanted to continue straight into the PhD
advice: Take a break and a relaxing holiday before starting a PhD and empty your to-do list
quote: In retrospect I should have taken a little holiday, even if it meant taking up a small loan.
author: DennisH

situation: Grad student excited about research but suffering stress-related problems
choice: Left grad school for a job doing work they equally enjoy
outcome: Knew it was the right decision; their employer is proud of having hired them away from grad school
main_reason: Stress, and a job that allowed them to do something else they enjoy
advice: Look at what else is out there and do not worry about how an incomplete degree looks
quote: Having left grad school for stress-related reasons myself, I can tell you I don't regret leaving at all.
author: BevTheDev

situation: Strong master's graduate who, because of covid, moved to a similar master's and did averagely because of personal problems
choice: Applied for PhDs after a weaker second master's
outcome: Three years later got a PhD position in a similar field with support from their first thesis advisor
main_reason: Moved master's because of covid
quote: Update: Managed to get a PhD! 3 years later.
author: Alex

situation: PhD student in the third year whose supervisor said they could finish early and become his postdoc instead
choice: Finished the PhD early and became their PI's postdoc, then moved into a faculty position
outcome: A few months into the faculty job they feel very well prepared and have had an excellent experience so far
main_reason: Productive research and a supervisor open to finishing early
quote: my n=1 experience with this unusual plan, at least, has been excellent so far.
author: half-pass

situation: PhD student writing their thesis who spent spare time on painting and drumming alone
choice: Focused on research and hobbies rather than networking, public speaking or leadership
outcome: Feels guilty about skills and CV-building they could have gained
main_reason: Stayed in their comfort zone
quote: I am currently writing my PhD thesis and I was feeling guilty about the things and skills I could have attained during this period but I didn't.
author: Cccr

situation: PhD student in computational modeling of 3D printing who wanted to do experimental work
choice: Completed a computational PhD in 5.5 years with four first-author papers
outcome: Now struggles to get a postdoc that combines experiments and simulation and regrets not picking an experimental topic
main_reason: Could not find a good experimental PhD topic
quote: Looking back, I do regret not choosing an experential topic.
author: rcive

situation: Started a PhD that turned out not to be a good fit
choice: Left the program at an advanced stage
outcome: Is at peace with the decision and thinks it strengthens a new PhD application
main_reason: The program was not a good fit
quote: I am personally secure with this decision and think that in some ways the experience even strengthens my application
author: Robert

situation: Young self-taught programmer doing paid work outside normal channels, before or instead of a traditional job
choice: Find clients who need business solutions and a mentor who can send work
outcome: The author found all kinds of paid programming work as a teenager by going to small businesses and programmer groups
main_reason: Businesses want working solutions, not just code
advice: Learn how the business works (books, shipping, order tracking), find a mentor who can farm work out to you, target businesses that have been through many programmers, and ignore HR and recruiters
quote: Don't focus on organizations, find people that want what you do. Forget HR and recruiters - they are of no help.
author: Meredith Poor

situation: Career changer with a nine-month stretch that ended on bad terms
choice: Decide whether to list that stretch on the resume
outcome: A long gap can raise red flags and some hiring managers screen it out, but being open about it works
main_reason: Employers worry about unexplained gaps
advice: Include the experience if it is relevant, explain it simply in the interview, and never hide it or lie
quote: And most importantly don't try to hide it or lie.
author: glacier

situation: Developer weighing whether to stay in programming after a painful job loss
choice: Decide what they want to be, based on what they actually do for fun
outcome: Their own history shows what they love; the author has programmed for fun for 27 years
main_reason: What you do shows what you love better than what you say
advice: Figure out what you want to be from your history, dust yourself off or move on, and learn from the experience
quote: 1) figure out what you want to be (from your personal history), 2) dust yourself off and get back up on the horse or move on if programming isn't for you, and 3) reflect and learn whatever there is to learn from this experience.
author: bob

situation: Junior developer at a first job with no mentoring or code review
choice: The author stayed far longer than they should have
outcome: They fell behind on key skills and technologies, which cost them
main_reason: Felt grateful just to have a decent paying job
advice: If the job lacks mentorship and a good tech stack, start looking for one where you can grow instead of hoping to change the place
quote: Don't fall into the trap of thinking that you might magically change this place for the better. Simply start looking for a job which will allow you to grow.
author: AndreiROM

situation: Employee with a job offer that pays about $20K more than the current job
choice: Accept the new offer first, then resign
outcome: Counteroffers rarely match the gap or materialize, so you can leave with dignity
main_reason: Raises are small and tied to inflation, not to the market
advice: Sign the new offer, then hand in your resignation; if your boss counters and falls short, move on
quote: Accept the offer. When you have the documents signed, go to your boss and hand in your letter of resignation.
author: AndreiROM

situation: Physics major who changed to a technically driven humanities major, and now works in a job they hate
choice: Switched from physics to a humanities major
outcome: Seven years later wants to get back to math graduate studies but has poor grades and no recommendations
quote: I made what I now consider the mistake of changing to a technically driven humanities major (Electronic Media, Arts and Communications)
author: Robare Pruyn

situation: Chemistry graduate who started a PhD during a very tough period and chose an advisor and program under stress
choice: Started a chemical engineering PhD in a field far from their background
outcome: Fifth year, struggling constantly and feeling like a failure
main_reason: Looked for stability while in a bad emotional place
quote: It was a bad choice, and I regret it deeply.
author: novelnow

situation: PhD student with a problematic supervisor, one of several students in the same situation
choice: Quit and reapplied to a PhD program in a different field, the one from their undergraduate major
outcome: Currently in the fourth year of the new program, and all the students in that situation are doing OK
main_reason: Problematic supervisor
advice: Try talking to your supervisor, then consider another supervisor, group or school, or leaving without shame
quote: I quit to reapply a Ph.D. program in a different field (also my major in undergrad) and currently 4th year in the new program.
author: user22080

situation: PhD student with an abusive PI who is unlikely to be punished
choice: Leave rather than wait for the PI to change
outcome: The author's former adviser lost 8-10 more students in two years and was still honored by the university
main_reason: You cannot base your decision on a PI changing
advice: Assume the abuse will continue and leave; such situations are shockingly common
quote: In my personal experience, there is no way the situation will get better.
author: roalddahl14

situation: Mathematician reflecting on changing research fields often
choice: Change fields or branch out regularly
outcome: The mathematician says it works: it keeps you growing and from being locked in
main_reason: A creative thinker is alive only while growing
advice: You do not have to change fields, but keep branching out and learning new things
quote: A creative thinker is alive only so long as he grows; you have to keep learning new things to understand the old.
author: Brauer Suzuki

situation: Employee thinking about quitting, worried about leaving their employer in a bind
choice: Quit in a way that does not burn bridges
outcome: Employers know people can leave at any time, so planning for your departure is their problem, not yours
main_reason: Look out for your own best interests
advice: Do not announce you might leave until you have a firm offer; once you give notice, do not let them pressure you into overtime or extra duties
quote: First and foremost, it's always okay to quit.
author: dwizum

situation: Employee deciding whether to give notice when quitting
choice: Treat the notice period as relationship management
outcome: Quitting without notice usually costs a good reference, goodwill, and the chance to list the job as a success
main_reason: Giving notice protects your reputation
advice: Take the long view and preserve your options; resign with notice unless you have overriding reasons
quote: However, you should look at this as a relationship-management issue rather than a legal one.
author: CodeGnome

situation: Employee deciding when and how to resign
choice: Try to fix the problem first, check the job market, then resign with a plan
outcome: A documented attempt to fix things shows it was their fault, not yours
main_reason: Make a confident decision after trying to fix the problem
advice: Read your contract for notice and non-competes, document attempts to fix the issue, and prepare answers for exit questions
quote: Most people recommend having a signed offer in hand, but if the job market looks good and you have a decent financial runway, that's fine too.
author: Hilmar

situation: Employee burned by a verbal promise of advancement that never took shape
choice: Find a new job instead of staying with a dishonest employer
outcome: The author says they were in the exact same shoes and that a dishonest company eventually makes your life hell
main_reason: The employer broke a verbal agreement
advice: Never commit to an offer until it is in writing and keep a copy; then find new employment
quote: Promise yourself that you won't commit to an offer until it's in writing.
author: Travis

situation: Employee tempted by a new job opportunity at another company
choice: Ask the boss for the chance to pursue it
outcome: If you can afford the worst case, you should go for it, but your standing may change once you ask
main_reason: Do not regret not trying
advice: Ask yourself whether you can afford to be unemployed and whether you will regret not trying; then be open with your boss
quote: If you can indeed afford the worst case scenario (having to pack your bag and seek out new opportunities) then you should totally go for it.
author: Jonast92

situation: Early-career developer unhappy with pay and thinking of moving jobs
choice: Stay and build skills unless a more interesting job appears
outcome: As your skills grow you become worth more, and more interesting jobs usually pay better
main_reason: Pay should follow skills and interest
advice: Be patient, live on what you earn, and move only for a more interesting job, not just higher pay
quote: If you move, don't do it for higher pay. Do it because you found a more interesting job.
author: BobRodes

situation: Early career in Japan, severely underpaid compared with the market after getting a job offer paying about 80% more
choice: Told their boss about the better offer and stayed when he doubled their salary
outcome: Stayed a couple more years, then left the country and is still good friends with the former boss
main_reason: The boss offered a doubled salary to keep them
advice: A counteroffer can work and is not always a red flag
quote: Years later, I'm still good friends with my former boss
author: Thomas Wang

situation: Person deciding where to do a PhD
choice: Choose the PI, thesis topic and university carefully
outcome: If any of the three turns out badly, life can go through hell; two people with jobs ignored the author's warning, started anyway and dropped out in 2-3 years
main_reason: The PI, the topic and the university matter most
advice: Be very careful where and under whom you study, especially if you already have a job and family
quote: the most important aspects of doing a PhD are your PI, your thesis topic and the university itself.
author: polfosol

situation: Master's graduate deciding whether to go straight into a PhD
choice: Spend some time outside academia first
outcome: Time away would have rebuilt the author's hunger for studying; many unhappy PhD students stay because of sunk cost
main_reason: Studying fatigue is real and hard to predict
advice: Focus on getting through the PhD program itself, not only the admissions
quote: you shouldn't focus solely on getting through the PhD program admissions, but on getting through the PhD program itself.
author: AdrienF

situation: Student going back to grad school after working in industry
choice: Return to grad school after years of work
outcome: Those who had worked struggled more with coursework but knew better why they were there
main_reason: Experience gives purpose; research is still a new kind of work
advice: Show you can actually do research; lean on classmates, who struggle too
quote: those who had worked for a while struggled more with coursework because they were out of practice with the whole lectures/problem sets/exam routine.
author: Jon Custer

situation: Older person wanting to do a PhD
choice: Do a PhD as a mature student
outcome: The mature candidates the author knew all finished, and one became a full professor years later
main_reason: Age rarely matters in academia
advice: Go for it if you love the field and want to stay in academia; do not do it for the money
quote: If you are in it for money, don't do it.
author: Stefan

situation: Master's student who stopped before finishing the thesis
choice: Restart the master's later at a place that fits real interests
outcome: A colleague who left for a full-time job later finished a master's elsewhere and then a PhD
main_reason: Finish the loose end when the time feels right
advice: Explain carefully in your statement why you will finish this time
quote: Restart the master's degree when the time feels right for you at a place that will enable you to pursue your real interests.
author: trikeprof

situation: Researcher feeling dissatisfied and thinking of leaving academia
choice: Leave academia only for good reasons
outcome: Similar pressures exist outside academia; both leaving and staying are viable
main_reason: General dissatisfaction is not a great reason to leave if you are doing well
advice: Talk to friends before a therapist; consider the industry Plan B
quote: you will have similar pressures outside academia, so general dissatisfaction with things like this is not a great reason to leave academia if you are doing well.
author: Flounderer

situation: PhD student unsure about a career in academia
choice: Drop the PhD if there is no delight in it
outcome: Spending two weeks living each choice reveals which one you regret and which feels right
main_reason: Delight in learning is the real reason to do a PhD
advice: If there is no delight, drop it; if there is, pursue it wholeheartedly
quote: If there is no delight then if I were you I'd drop it at once.
author: Martin Kochanski

situation: Student unhappy in a PhD program straight after a master's
choice: Take time off to think it through
outcome: Starting something new often feels strange; if it is fundamentally wrong you will not adapt
main_reason: A year off after the master's would have helped
advice: Step back and contemplate whether the program is right at a deep level
quote: In hindsight, it might have been better to take a year off after your master’s.
author: Eggy

situation: PhD student in a low-performing group whose advisor showed no interest in their own workable research idea
choice: Stayed with the advisor and group instead of moving sooner
outcome: Wasted a lot of time and effort, eventually changed advisors and changed direction so much that the first idea was lost
main_reason: Waited for an uninterested advisor
advice: Take your ideas to advisors who will actually work with you
quote: In short, I was complicit in wasting a lot of my own time and effort.
author: Anonymous

situation: Community college graduate accepted into both linguistics programs and an agriculture program
choice: Chose the agriculture program over linguistics, mostly because it let them stay in their hometown
outcome: Failed badly in the first year, worked for two and a half years, then enrolled in linguistics, did very well, earned a master's and started a PhD
main_reason: Stayed near home instead of moving for the program they wanted
advice: Graduate schools care more about your ability in the subject you apply for than about your overall record; be honest about past grades
quote: I got a full-time job and worked for two and a half years, but remained interested in linguistics and started to regret very strongly never entering a linguistics program.
author: Matt Menzenski

situation: Graduate student weighing a postdoc against going straight into industry
choice: Go into industry directly or do a postdoc to build skills
outcome: More graduate students now get industry jobs straight out of grad school, especially in biotech, often through contacts
main_reason: Industry hiring has opened up
advice: Do a postdoc only if you need skills or an industry-friendly lab; otherwise grow your network
quote: Having a great network of contacts is a key to a successful job search.
author: KK100

situation: Grad student deciding whether to quit or switch programs
choice: Decide whether grad school or just this program is wrong
outcome: Each choice has good answers you can defend in interviews
main_reason: Whichever you pick must be seated deep within you
advice: Talk to your advisor and department chair first, finish the semester, or take a one- or two-semester break
quote: There are good answers for every choice you can make here--you just have to believe in them enough to defend them without shame.
author: kmc

situation: Master's student doing well but doubting whether to try for a PhD
choice: Apply and see what happens
outcome: Difficulty is relative; if you fail at a career it is not the end of the world
main_reason: Not trying means a lifetime of wondering
advice: Apply to a PhD program and see what happens
quote: But if you never bother to even try, then you'll never know and you'll always have a "What if?" moment.
author: user7628

situation: Physics student choosing a PhD without thinking about jobs
choice: Think about job prospects before committing
outcome: Many classmates pursued the field they loved without looking at the odds of an academic career
main_reason: Faculty chances can be below 1 in 30
advice: Look at the CVs of professors in the field and have a plan B before starting
quote: Without a good plan B you stand behind I would not start or get talked into such an odyssey.
author: Hauser

situation: Person who graduated in 1984 and went back for a master's by research 25 years later, then a PhD
choice: Return to study after a long career
outcome: Industry experience gives resilience and a clear reason for studying
main_reason: Life experience helps with stress and focus
advice: Expect reading and writing papers to be tough at first, and use your real-world perspective
quote: You'll probably have more resiliency than your fellow students, due to your life experience.
author: mhwombat

situation: Author changed careers from IT to a different field eight years ago.
choice: The author switched from an IT career to a completely different field.
outcome: The author lost their job in the new field and returned to IT temporarily.
main_reason: The author determined the previous line of work was not for them.
advice: Be honest in interviews about career gaps and emphasize applicable skills on the resume.
author: Keith

situation: Mechanical engineer worked in test engineering and construction, then discovered programming through automation tasks.
choice: Switched careers from engineering to programming after taking CS classes and attending a career fair.
outcome: Loved the initial transition but now struggles with poor documentation and legacy code in a corporate role.
main_reason: Developed a strong interest in programming while automating repetitive engineering tasks.
advice: First job does not define career; pursue interests and seek opportunities to switch if desired.
quote: Fast forward two years and I'm trying to hang on to that passion as hard as I can, because my job is sucking it all away.
author: yankees13

situation: they were an unhappy lecturer in biostatistics after completing their PhD, feeling restless and dissatisfied with academic pressures.
choice: they quit their lectureship, moved countries, took a data‑science job, then left that job to become self‑employed and take a part‑time academic role.
outcome: they now work as a self‑employed freelancer combining academic research with entrepreneurship, feeling independent and satisfied with their work.
main_reason: they were unhappy with the academic environment and wanted more freedom and ownership of their research.
advice: they suggest persisting through early setbacks, not burning bridges, and being open to returning to academia later if needed.
quote: Leaving academia was the best thing I ever did, but be prepared for a shock to the system as you enter the "real world".
author: SoB

situation: they had just completed their PhD and were considering a field switch
choice: they switched fields shortly after their PhD
outcome: they entered an expanding field where their previous experience is valuable
main_reason: to move into a rapidly expanding field where their prior expertise would be an asset
advice: enter a fast‑growing area where your existing knowledge adds value and switch before reaching tenure‑track stages
quote: I switched fields shortly after my PhD into an expanding field, which is quite a common move for that field.
author: Wrzlprmft

situation: They taught biology students during their PhD in physics and later left academia after completing the degree.
choice: They decided to leave academia and pursue a job in industry.
outcome: Twenty‑five years later they work in industry and use their physics knowledge to help their children with math and physics.
main_reason: They felt academic teaching was disconnected from real‑world needs and wanted a more practical career.
advice: Simplify teaching to what learners need and focus on practical relevance.
quote: I left academia after my PhD and went into industry. It is now 25 years and I am faced with math and physics again when helping my children.
author: WoJ

situation: He was a PhD student who was publicly insulted and harassed by a senior professor.
choice: He decided to leave academia.
outcome: He left academia and later reflects on the decision.
main_reason: The professor's harassment and the medieval academic culture.
advice: If you choose to fight, make sure you enjoy it because it will be very tough.
quote: I left academia mostly for this.
author: WoJ

situation: they held a doctorate in mathematics and faced a poor job market for mathematicians
choice: they switched to computer science by taking a summer program for formal instruction
outcome: they acquired a CS background and changed their career direction
main_reason: the limited job prospects for mathematicians
advice: they should get a suitable job in the new field and avoid pursuing a second doctorate
quote: My doctorate is in math, but I switched to CS due to a poor market for mathematicians.
author: Buffy

situation: The author felt pressure in academia that leaving implied failure.
choice: The author left academia to pursue other intellectual pursuits.
outcome: The author is much happier and freer to write and learn.
main_reason: The author was not fulfilled in their academic position.
advice: Academic jobs are just jobs, so look for a different job if unfulfilled.
quote: I left academia 8 years ago and am much happier and (ironically) freer to pursue various intellectual pursuits, such as writing and learning about different things.
author: Kaushik Ghose

situation: She was an academic researcher feeling pressure to become a PI and worried about external validation.
choice: She left academia and became a clinician.
outcome: She now works as a clinician, does occasional research, enjoys broader conversations, and no longer tracks citations.
main_reason: She did not relish leading a research group and wanted to avoid feeling like a failure.
advice: Make like Elsa and let it go, releasing the need for external validation.
quote: I still lurk on Academia SO because I like to be reminded that my decision was right :)
author: Ottie

situation: The author completed a 5.5‑year PhD in a theoretical field with three publications and then spent four more years in academia as a postdoc.
choice: They decided to leave academia and take a job in industry.
outcome: They are now working in industry, continue to publish research, and are very happy with the job.
main_reason: Postdoc jobs have low pay, poor work‑life balance, and limited entry barriers, making industry more attractive.
quote: After that I went to industry, I continue to do and to publish research and I'm very happy with my current job.
author: qbit-

situation: After two years of temporary academic positions, the author decided to leave academia.
choice: They chose to move into a cybersecurity career instead of staying in research.
outcome: They now work in cybersecurity, using communication skills, and continue math research as a hobby without academic pressures.
main_reason: Better salary and flexibility for independent research.
advice: Industry jobs can fund research and provide time freedom; staying in academia isn’t the only path to continue math.
quote: I left academia after two years of temporary positions, eventually migrating to a career in cybersecurity.
author: Jeremy Dover

situation: He completed a PhD in physics and was working within academia.
choice: He decided to leave academia because he felt he would never be a very good physicist.
outcome: He is now outside of academia and reflects on his studies positively.
main_reason: He believed he would never be a very good physicist despite loving teaching.
advice: Talk with physicists at average, local universities to get a realistic view of the job.
quote: I left academia after my PhD because I knew I would never be a very good physicist (though I loved to teach).
author: WoJ

situation: They finished their doctorate when there were no hiring opportunities for mathematicians.
choice: They switched to computer science, considering accounting as an alternative.
outcome: Their career suffered, but they remained not disillusioned with mathematics.
main_reason: Lack of academic and workplace positions for mathematicians.
quote: But, though my career suffered, I wasn't disillusioned with math itself.
author: Buffy

situation: they completed a PhD in theoretical computer science and were seeking employment
choice: they accepted a tech writer position in industry
outcome: after a few months they moved to a coding role
main_reason: their advisor’s recommendation and their ability to learn quickly
advice: research teaching jobs as a bridge and leverage the PhD as a plus in relevant domains
quote: I did a PhD in theoretical computer science, and then switched to a job in industry.
author: Gilles 'SO- stop being evil'

situation: They left academia and had years of notes stored in folders and boxes.
choice: They decided the notes were pointless clutter and dumped them in the recycling.
outcome: They never looked at the notes again and now rely on books or online sources for information.
main_reason: The notes were seen as unnecessary clutter.
advice: Consider discarding old academic materials that no longer serve a purpose.
quote: I never looked at any of those notes again. Eventually, I just decided that they were pointless clutter and dumped them in the recycling.
author: Simon B

situation: they were an academic researcher considering moving to industry
choice: they decided to leave academia for an industrial research position
outcome: they say everything worked out well and they continue to write papers
main_reason: they wanted a change despite fear of leaving academia
advice: they advise not being afraid of change and staying involved in conferences
quote: everything worked out well, and I even get to writ
author: joe the publisher

situation: they resigned from a small company after a year, citing a desire for a higher position in a different field and a relationship with a coworker
choice: they decided to leave for a higher position in a different field
outcome: they left on good terms with everyone, but now face an awkward invitation to a company event as a significant other
main_reason: they wanted to work in their desired field and advance their career
quote: I left on good terms with everyone.
author: BelethorsGeneralGoods

situation: Author left academia in 1990 to join industry after failing to find an academic job.
choice: Chose to work in industry instead of pursuing an academic career.
outcome: Income increased substantially and career was established, but feelings of loss persist.
main_reason: Academic jobs were unavailable for their specific field, and industry offered better income.
advice: Focus on making the best of current choices rather than dwelling on past opportunities.
quote: But my teeth hurt when I gritted my teeth and said no. If I didn't have a mortgage then, I would been severely tempted go back to fresh-caught prof wages.
author: Dan

situation: The author was in a top psychology PhD program during the second year.
choice: They quit the program halfway through the second year due to theoretical disagreements with professors.
outcome: They faced identity crisis, family reactions, and difficulty finding a job, eventually securing research coordinator positions after adjusting their resume and interviewing for entry‑level roles.
main_reason: Theoretical disagreements with professors and lack of fit with the program.
advice: Use a community career center to create a concise resume, withdraw fully from the program, research the new field, and be prepared to explain the departure honestly.
quote: I was still on my school’s website as a doctoral student and I was formally on a leave of absence, which was discordant with the “withdrew in good standing” statement on my resume. This created suspicion that I was just on a break from my program and probably contributed to being turned down.
author: Yolanda

situation: They entered an R1 math program in the 1960s with a fellowship and made little progress.
choice: They switched to another university and took a TA position to complete their PhD.
outcome: They finished the degree in three years and became highly knowledgeable in their area.
main_reason: A better advisor and teaching duties gave them insight and motivation.
quote: I also gained better insight into a small area of math and became, in the words of my advisor, "the most knowledgeable person in the world in ..."
author: Buffy

situation: Author was in a PhD program approaching their 30s with financial and family pressures.
choice: Left the PhD program and entered the job market with a Master's degree.
outcome: Secured a great job, achieved a happy marriage, and is buying a house.
main_reason: Prioritized family future and financial stability over academic pride.
advice: Consider if pride is worth your family's future before continuing a long program.
quote: I've got a happy marriage, a great job, and I'm buying a house within the next two years, so.
author: Umbrella_Programmer

situation: Author finished a master's degree and considered pursuing a Ph.D. for a research career.
choice: Author decided to leave academia and enter industry instead of starting a Ph.D. program.
outcome: Author is very happy in industry and avoids the stress of a demanding doctoral program.
main_reason: Author did not want a research career and valued personal happiness over academic prestige.
advice: Evaluate your true motivations for a Ph.D. and ensure you genuinely want a research career.
quote: I am very happy now and can't imagine how stressed out and miserable I would be if I were forcing myself to go through years of a Ph.D.
author: Kevin

situation: The author turned down a PhD offer from their undergraduate advisor and left the PhD program, now taking a gap year.
choice: They decided to quit the PhD program.
outcome: They are currently on a gap year and have had mixed reactions from interviewers.
main_reason: Feeling dissatisfied with the program, advisor, and personal life balance.
quote: I've turned down a PhD offer from my undergraduate advisor this year and currently I'm taking a gap year.
author: user10517213

situation: The author had a Master's in Environmental Engineering and applied for PhDs in related fields but was rejected.
choice: They applied to and accepted a PhD position in Biology, a field different from their previous studies.
outcome: They completed the PhD and found their previous skills in programming and statistics helpful in the new field.
main_reason: The research project sounded interesting and was related to an existing hobby.
advice: Apply broadly to fields where your skills are useful, but only enter a PhD if you truly want to work there.
quote: I have found that skills I picked up in my earlier fields (among them programming and statistics) have been very helpful to me in biology
author: brendan

situation: The author left a PhD program and entered industry work in the US.
choice: Quit the PhD to pursue a software engineering job.
outcome: Has been working as a software engineer at a big‑tech company for about 2.5 years.
main_reason: Believed a PhD was unnecessary for industry and wanted relevant technical experience.
advice: A PhD is not required for tech jobs; focus on experience and a master’s degree is sufficient.
quote: It’s been about 2 and a half years that I started working in industry in the US, after I quit my PhD and got a Master's degree (though I had another Master's before joining the PhD program).
author: Mithridates the Great

situation: they were a PhD student experiencing ups and downs and felt unable to continue
choice: they decided to quit their PhD program
outcome: they left the program and later received another opportunity a few years afterward
main_reason: they felt the situation was untenable and chose to quit
advice: they suggest talking to supervisors or department staff before quitting, as it can be a turning point
quote: Full disclosure: I quit my PhD. The first my supervisor heard of it was the day I quit. Luckily, someone else gave me another chance a few years later.
author: Dave Clarke

situation: Author left a mechanical engineering PhD to work, then decided to return to graduate school.
choice: They chose to re-enter graduate school and switch research focus to robotics.
outcome: They joined a multidisciplinary robotics group and are glad about the change despite age concerns.
main_reason: They enjoyed coding and instrumentation more than their original experimental fluid mechanics focus.
advice: They suggest joining multidisciplinary research groups to combine interests if changing fields.
quote: Personally, I'm extremely glad I made the change. I like the field much better and my research is much more interesting
author: somerandomdude

situation: The author was a pure math grad student who lost interest in the subject when starting their dissertation.
choice: They switched from a pure math PhD to an applied math PhD.
outcome: They found the new field more enjoyable and inspiring, leading to greater overall happiness.
main_reason: They did not enjoy the pure math subject enough to continue for the long term.
advice: Grit has limits in a PhD, so switching fields is better than suffering for decades.
quote: I switched to doing an applied math PhD and have found it personally to be much better. I enjoy the subject a lot more, feel more inspired in the field of research, and am ultimately a lot happier.
author: Vladhagen

situation: They have finished five years of a PhD with five top‑tier publications that are unrelated, making a thesis impossible and losing their scholarship.
choice: They decided to complete the PhD by submitting two recent papers and obtaining the advisor’s permission.
outcome: If the two papers are published, they will be allowed to submit a thesis and receive a project assistantship salary while finishing.
main_reason: They care about earning the PhD and want to avoid leaving without it, and the advisor agreed to support the plan.
advice: Complete the PhD without antagonizing the advisor and wait for the two papers to be published.
quote: I have decided to complete my PhD without antagonizing my advisor.
author: user2808118

situation: Student struggled with serious health issues affecting PhD progress and feared negative perception.
choice: Left the PhD program after two years instead of discussing health problems with the advisor.
outcome: Received an M.S. last year with disability services help, but deeply regrets leaving the PhD program.
main_reason: Fear of how the advisor and department would perceive the health issues and affect career.
advice: Open a dialogue with students and encourage them to seek assistance from disability services offices.
quote: Personally, I left my PhD program after two years rather than discuss my ongoing health problems with my advisor. I deeply regret that decision.
author: IndigoJNight

situation: The author faced abusive treatment and belittling from a foreman at a new construction job.
choice: They quit the job immediately after two days without giving notice.
outcome: They found a better job within 30 minutes and the boss likely addressed the foreman's behavior.
main_reason: The foreman was abusive, assigned impossible tasks, and belittled the author in front of others.
advice: Sign up with multiple temp agencies to ensure quick employment if you need to leave a toxic environment.
quote: Ironically, less than 30 minutes after I quit, I was on my way to a different job where I was better treated.
author: Taylor

situation: The author resigned from their job in Toronto to accept a written offer from a UK company.
choice: They quit their current job to start a new position with the UK company.
outcome: The new office was not ready, the start date became indefinite, and the author became unemployed.
main_reason: They accepted a written job offer and resigned from their previous employment.
advice: Stop blaming the company, accept responsibility for the risk, and immediately start a new job search.
quote: The date arrived and the new office was nowhere to be found. The UK company had failed to get their new location going.
author: user7360

situation: they were hired at a low rate and were promised a raise after passing probation
choice: they quit their job to work elsewhere after the promised raise was not delivered
outcome: they left the company and secured a higher‑pay position elsewhere
main_reason: the employer failed to honor the promised raise
advice: always get important promises in writing and don’t rely on a verbal agreement
quote: The sad truth is that if it's not in the contract, consider it a lie.
author: ptr

situation: Author was a Senior Developer at a small startup with limited growth opportunities.
choice: They quit to become a Software Engineer at a larger company with more resources.
outcome: They became a Tech Lead and Senior Software Engineer within a year.
main_reason: Desire for opportunities to work in a larger environment with more manpower.
advice: Practice telling a story about the job title change that does not rely solely on salary.
quote: At the new employer, I was able to be a Tech Lead and did so on many projects, and became a "Senior Software Engineer" within a year of working there.
author: Joe

situation: The author worked remotely for a company with unreliable and delayed payments.
choice: They quit their job after realizing the owner did not care about employees.
outcome: The company went under one month after they left, affecting other workers.
main_reason: The owner's lack of care and financial instability signaled the company was failing.
advice: Send out resumes and leave the job immediately if payments are unreliable.
quote: I left my job and a month later, the company went under, taking all the other workers with it.
author: Newbie

situation: The author was the sole developer on multiple projects, working excessive unpaid hours and suffering from severe anxiety and physical symptoms.
choice: They resigned from their job to escape the toxic work environment and find a healthier workplace.
outcome: They took a break, then joined a startup with reasonable hours and a higher salary.
main_reason: The author was experiencing severe stress, anxiety, and physical health issues due to overwork and lack of support.
advice: Leave the job immediately because the company will not change, and better opportunities with fairer conditions are available elsewhere.
quote: I left, took a couple months to cool down, then walked straight into a small startup company and found myself on sensible 9 - 5 hours and earning about 3k more.
author: Ruadhan2300

situation: The author was offered a promotion with a promised salary increase that was later denied by the employer.
choice: The author resigned immediately after the employer refused to honor the salary agreement.
outcome: The author secured a much more lucrative role almost immediately after leaving.
main_reason: The author viewed the denial of the promised salary as a major breach of trust.
advice: Decide whether money or experience is more important before accepting a promotion.
quote: I resigned immediately and ended up securing a much more lucrative role almost immediately.
author: ChrisFNZ

situation: they were working as a developer and considering leaving their job
choice: they decided to resign from their position
outcome: they resigned a few months ago and completed a transition plan
main_reason: they wanted a new job and to finish their current project before leaving
advice: they recommend having a new job lined up and creating a detailed transition plan before resigning
quote: I resigned from a job a few months ago.
author: Matthew Gaiser

situation: They needed to resign in Germany before the end of the month to avoid an extra month of notice, but HR was absent from the office.
choice: They arranged a meeting with HR, told them they wanted to leave at the end of the notice period, and sent a scanned resignation for confirmation.
outcome: HR accepted the resignation, sent a confirmation, and the original copy was delivered to HR through a colleague.
main_reason: To avoid an additional month of notice period.
advice: Schedule a meeting with HR, send a scanned resignation for written confirmation, and have the original delivered by a colleague.
author: GeologicalWren

situation: They were a new contractor in the US working through multiple staffing agencies and were paid a very low wage.
choice: They decided to quit the job because the pay was too low.
outcome: They left the position, the boss at Company D was understanding, and HR warned them about discussing wages.
main_reason: low wage
quote: When I quit the Company C/D job I informed the boss that my wage was the only reason I was leaving.
author: lilydi989898

situation: They worked five years at a well‑known institution with high workloads, sexism, and a blame culture.
choice: They decided to quit their job.
outcome: They are preparing for a final meeting with their boss and worry about receiving a recommendation and being blamed for a project hand‑off.
main_reason: Toxic combination of overwork, sexism, and lack of support for women.
advice: Their teenage daughter suggested they talk about how great a manager he is and the good projects they have done.
quote: My boss and I are having a final meeting.
author: angela

situation: They were working under a manager who wanted them gone and were eventually fired, and later they quit another job because of a senior colleague’s dislike.
choice: They decided to quit the job after the senior person’s behavior and the manager’s hostility.
outcome: They left the company; their boss acknowledged the senior’s dislike and tried to lure them to stay, which upset them but also made them smile.
main_reason: A senior colleague’s dislike and a hostile manager made the work environment untenable.
advice: Start a job search immediately, improve marketable skills, stay upbeat, volunteer for extra work, and align discussions with manager’s goals without appearing as a complainer.
quote: He also said something like "you've done such a great (and visible) job on the XXX project over the past 9 months that every time Steve bad-mouths you, he looks like an idiot. If you leave that stops".
author: Flydog57

situation: They resigned and their last day fell on a public holiday, and the new employer wanted to move the end date earlier.
choice: They refused to change the end date, stating it would become a termination/dismissal.
outcome: The employer eventually paid them for the holiday, albeit grudgingly.
main_reason: To avoid being treated as a termination and facing an unfair dismissal claim.
advice: Check contract terms and push back on last‑day changes that affect pay or rights.
quote: I firmly said if they took such action, it would no longer be resignation and would instead be termination/dismissal, which would be met with an unfair dismissal claim (as this was in Australia).
author: fabspro

situation: They were hired urgently as a technical support engineer for a several‑month project.
choice: They resigned after one week on the job.
outcome: This caused the outsourcing company to be obligated to pay a penalty for their client.
main_reason: They felt the amount of technical debt and underestimated hardware capacities were too large.
quote: This caused the outsoursing company to be obligated to pay a penalty for their client.
author: mltm

situation: they resigned from a company they had fun at and made many friends
choice: they decided to leave the company despite feeling it didn’t feel right
outcome: they now have a job that fits them better, feel better, and the previous company is running fine
main_reason: they wanted a role that better fits their preferences
advice: stay professional, don’t burn bridges, ask for referrals, thank the boss for the opportunity
quote: But now I have a job that fits me better, I feel better and my previous company is running just fine.
author: Kevin

situation: they were a software developer at a large corporate and felt the need for a change
choice: they quit their job without another one lined up
outcome: they spent four months traveling in South‑East Asia, are up‑skilling in web and mobile development, and are doing freelance work and a startup project
main_reason: they wanted flexibility to travel, learn new skills, and pursue personal projects
advice: they suggest reducing hours or finding part‑time work before quitting, networking, building an online profile, and confirming if a Silicon Valley job is truly desired
quote: Since then, I've spent 4 months travelling in South-East Asia. Now, I'm up-skilling in web and mobile development so I can either freelance or get part-time work in a smaller company.
author: Will J Thomas

situation: they were employed at a company that did not meet their expectations
choice: they resigned from the job
outcome: they worked through the notice period but the company refused to give a proper reference
main_reason: the company failed to meet their expectations
advice: focus on what they learned during the stay, as the experience is better than starting with nothing
quote: The company did not meet my expectations so I resigned.
author: Jonast92

situation: they resigned from a job and their last day fell on a holiday
choice: they submitted a resignation with the holiday as the final date
outcome: the HR department paid them for the holiday days
main_reason: they wanted to leave the job
advice: do not accept a resignation date that falls on a holiday and ensure the employer pays up to the actual last working day
quote: As it happens this is exactly what happened when I resigned from a job once. They didn't notice at the time I submitted my resignation that my last day was a holiday and their HR insisted they pay me for it.
author: HLGEM
